title: Amplified Home Phones: Loud Ringers, Big Buttons and Easier Calls
subtitle: A plain-English guide to corded and cordless landline phones that make callers louder, ring louder and are easier to dial.
excerpt: If phone calls have turned into a guessing game, an amplified home phone may help you hear callers better. Here is what these phones can and cannot do, what the listed prices were, and what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Maybe you have missed a call because the ringer was too soft. Maybe a grandchild's voice sounds muffled, and you find yourself saying "What was that?" more than you would like. For many people, the home phone is still the main way family, doctors and pharmacies get in touch, so a call you cannot hear is a real problem.

An amplified phone is a home phone built to make the caller's voice louder than a regular phone can. Most also have a very loud ringer, a flashing light when a call comes in, and big buttons that are easier to see and press.

Loudness is measured in decibels, or dB. On these phones, the number tells you how much extra volume the phone can add to the caller's voice. The models below list different maximums: up to 40 dB for the ClearSounds CSC500, up to 50 dB for the Serene CL-65 and the Panasonic KX-TGM450S, and up to 55 dB for the Serene HD-60. Some also let you adjust tone, so you can make voices sound deeper or higher, whichever is easier for your ears.

You can choose a corded phone, which sits on a desk or hangs on the wall, or a cordless phone, which you can carry from room to room. Some cordless sets can add extra handsets so there is a phone in the kitchen and the bedroom.

If you wear hearing aids, look for a phone labeled hearing-aid compatible. Some hearing aids have a telecoil, or T-coil, a small part meant to connect with compatible phones. The FCC's consumer guide says phones covered by its rules should minimize noise and work with T-coils. It also says something about volume:
"Wireline telephones and wireless handsets also provide volume control within prescribed amplification limits." (FCC consumer guide, fcc.gov)

Be clear about the limits. These phones boost call audio only. They do not help you hear conversation in a room or the television, and they are not hearing aids. Before relying on any amplification, it makes sense to have your hearing tested by an audiologist, and to ask that person whether a particular phone will work with your hearing aids.

items: Amplification you can switch off. A phone set loud enough for you may be too loud for a spouse or visitor. The Serene and Panasonic phones include a way to turn amplification off and on as needed.
A loud ringer plus a flashing light. A visual ringer helps if you are in another room or have the TV on.
Big, clear buttons. One-touch memory buttons for family and doctors save dialing. Some phones have photo buttons, so you press a picture instead of a number.
Talking caller ID. Some cordless phones read out who is calling, which helps if the screen is hard to read.
Battery backup. Backup batteries are often optional and not included. The Serene HD-60 page says that without batteries the phone works during an outage but loses amplification.

Your phone line. These phones need a working landline or a compatible line. Serene's FAQ says DSL internet on the same line needs a filter, and ClearSounds says its phone does not work with high-speed dedicated business internet.

Hearing-aid compatibility claims. Panasonic's page says the KX-TGM450S meets the TIA-1083 hearing-aid compatibility standard, and ClearSounds describes the CSC500 as FCC hearing-aid compatible. Those are the sellers' own statements, so confirm with your audiologist.
No monthly fee from the phone itself. None of the pages list a subscription, but you still pay for your own phone service, which the pages do not price.
Stock and returns. In November 2026 all of these product pages showed the phones as sold out, so check availability, current price and the return policy before you count on a particular phone.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Dial-tone and setup problems are common topics in the help pages we found, so plan on some help. It is worth having a family member or handy friend connect the phone, make a test call, and confirm the dial tone works.

While your helper is there, save the most important numbers to the one-touch buttons: family, your doctor's office, your pharmacy. Try the amplify and tone settings during a real call to find what sounds best to you. If the phone takes backup batteries, put them in now, and use the type the maker specifies; Serene, for example, says to use rechargeable batteries only in the CL-65.
Finally, think about placement. Put the base where you usually sit, and if you choose a cordless set, consider an extra handset near the bed.

A Help or speakerphone button on a home phone is just a phone key. The Serene CL-65's Help button makes a hands-free call, but its page describes no monitoring service, so it is not a medical alert system. In an emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A louder, simpler phone will not fix every hearing challenge, but it may make calls a little easier. Pick the features that match the trouble you actually have, check that the phone is in stock, and ask someone to help with setup.

products.name: ClearSounds CSC500 Amplified Large Button Speakerphone w/Photo Frame Buttons
products.price: Sale $79.95 (regular $89.95, November 2026); shipping calculated at checkout. Listed as sold out, so check current price
products.blurb: May suit someone who would rather press a picture than dial a number, with 8 photo buttons and 3 memory keys. Amplification is 15 dB by default and up to 40 dB with the AMPLIFY key, though the page says the maximum varies with home line power; the ringer reaches 85 dB and a light flashes for calls.

products.name: Serene Innovations HD-60 Amplified Phone (corded)
products.price: Regular $149.95 (November 2026). Listed as sold out, so check current price
products.blurb: Suits a household where one person needs it loud and others do not: amplification is 37 to 55 dB with amplify on and 0 to 18 dB with it off. It has 12 memory buttons, a ringer up to 95 dBA, flashing lights and an off-hook alert that warns if the handset is not seated.

products.name: Serene Innovations CL-65 Loud Cordless Phone
products.price: Regular $129.95 (November 2026). Listed as sold out, so check current price
products.blurb: For someone who wants to carry the phone around the house, with amplification up to 50 dB and talking caller ID in English or French. It has eight one-touch speed-dial buttons and can expand to four handsets, sold separately.

products.name: Panasonic KX-TGM450S Amplified Cordless Phone with Digital Answering Machine
products.price: Sale $203.99 (November 2026). Listed as sold out, so check current price
products.blurb: A fuller-featured choice with a built-in answering machine, a ringer up to 112 dB, voice amplification up to 50 dB and a 250-number call block. It also offers talking caller ID, a setting called Slow Talk, and room for up to six handsets.
